question: Where does the landing distance begin?
explanation: The landing is measured from 50 ft above the threshold to a complete stop. The 50 ft point is the landing screen height.

question: How does the landing screen height compare between aeroplane classes?

options.text: It is 50 ft for all classes
It is 50 ft for Class A and 35 ft for Class B
It is 35 ft for Class A and 50 ft for Class B

explanation: The landing screen height is fixed at 50 ft for all classes, unlike the take-off screen (35 ft Class A, 50 ft Class B).

question: What is the minimum VREF for a Class A aeroplane?

options.text: The greater of 1.3 VS0 and VMCA, plus 5 kt

explanation: For Class A, VREF must be no less than the greater of 1.23 × the landing configuration reference stall speed and VMCL.

question: What is the minimum VREF for aeroplanes other than Class A?
explanation: For other classes, VREF must be at least 1.3 × the stall speed in the landing configuration.

question: A Class A aeroplane has VSR0 of 120 kt and VMCL of 110 kt. What is its minimum VREF?
explanation: 1.23 × 120 = 147.6 kt, which is greater than VMCL (110 kt), so VREF is about 148 kt. Using the 1.3 factor gives 156 kt.

question: A Class B aeroplane has a landing configuration stall speed VS0 of 60 kt. What is its minimum VREF?
explanation: 1.3 × 60 = 78 kt. 1.23 × 60 (74 kt) is the Class A factor.

question: Why must the pilot be at VREF at the landing screen height?

options.text: The published landing distances assume it
It is the minimum control speed
It is the speed for best glide
It gives the best go-around climb

explanation: Landing distances in the flight manual are based on crossing the screen at VREF. Any other speed means the published distance will not be achieved.

question: About how long is the airborne section of a landing, from 50 ft to touchdown?
explanation: The airborne section, from the screen height to main-wheel touchdown, is usually taken as about 1 000 ft.

question: What happens in the landing flare?

options.text: Thrust is increased and the nose lowered
Thrust is reduced to idle and the pitch increased slightly
The gear is lowered and flaps retracted
Reverse thrust is selected in the air just before touchdown

explanation: In the flare (or round-out), thrust is reduced and the pitch attitude raised slightly to reduce the rate of descent and speed, so the main wheels touch first.

question: What is the landing distance required?

options.text: The airborne section plus the ground run
The landing distance available minus 1 000 ft
The distance from the threshold to touchdown

explanation: The landing distance required combines the airborne part from 50 ft and the ground roll to a stop. It must not exceed the landing distance available.

question: Where must the aeroplane be at 50 ft on the approach, for the landing distance to apply?

options.text: At the end of the approach lights

explanation: The landing distance starts at 50 ft directly over the threshold. Touching down on the threshold is not the aim.

question: Why is the LDA sometimes shorter than the paved runway?

options.text: It always excludes the first 300 m

explanation: The LDA runs from threshold to threshold; a displaced threshold, often because of approach obstacles, shortens it.

question: Why is lift harmful during the landing roll?

options.text: It reduces the load on the wheels and so the braking
It increases the reverse thrust needed

explanation: Lift takes load off the wheels and reduces brake effectiveness, so lift spoilers or dumpers are deployed after touchdown to destroy it.

question: How does a jet engine produce reverse thrust?

options.text: By shutting down the core and using the APU
By changing the blade angle of the fan
By redirecting the jet efflux forwards
By reversing the direction of the fan

explanation: Reversers redirect the exhaust or fan flow forwards to produce a rearward force.

question: Why is jet reverse thrust less effective than it might be?

options.text: It can only be used on dry runways, never on wet ones
Late to deploy, early to cancel

explanation: Interlocks need weight on the wheels and wheel spin-up, and reconfiguring takes time; it must also be cancelled at low speed, so the usable period is short.

question: Below about what speed must jet reverse thrust normally be cancelled?
explanation: At low speed the redirected gases can be re-ingested, raising engine temperatures and drawing in debris, so reverse is cancelled at around 50 kt.

question: How does propeller reverse thrust differ from jet reverse thrust?

options.text: It is weaker and cannot be used on wet runways
It is available sooner and can be used to a full stop
It takes longer to select and must be cancelled at 50 kt
It is only available in the air

explanation: Only a change of blade angle is needed, so reverse is available earlier and can be held to a full stop.

question: Why are landing regulations less demanding for turboprops than for jets?

options.text: Their reverse is usable for longer
Turboprops land at higher speeds than jets of similar size

explanation: The longer usable period of propeller reverse gives turboprops a braking advantage, so their landing distance factor is less severe.

question: What happens to induced drag once the nose wheel is on the runway?

options.text: It stays as in the approach

explanation: With the nose wheel down the angle of attack is almost nil, so induced drag virtually disappears.

question: How does parasite drag change during the landing roll?

options.text: It increases steadily all the way to the stop

explanation: Flaps, slats and spoilers give high parasite drag at touchdown, but it falls rapidly with speed, reaching zero at the stop.

question: How does wheel drag change during the landing roll?

options.text: It increases as the wheels load up

explanation: At touchdown the wing still carries much of the weight, so wheel drag is small. As speed falls and spoilers dump lift, wheel load and wheel drag rise.

question: Which retarding force is the most important in the landing roll?
explanation: Brake drag gives the greatest retarding force, but only when there is enough friction between tyres and runway.

question: Why should lift be destroyed as soon as possible after touchdown?

options.text: So the nose wheel can be steered
So the brakes become effective early
So reverse thrust can be selected

explanation: Brakes are only effective with sufficient wheel load and friction; dumping lift loads the wheels so braking is effective early in the roll.

question: Below about what fraction of the landing speed does brake drag provide most of the retarding force?
explanation: Early in the roll aerodynamic drag dominates; once speed falls below about 70% of the landing speed, brake drag provides most of the deceleration.

question: Which formula describes the stopping distance?
explanation: The stopping distance is V² ÷ 2d, with deceleration d = retarding force ÷ mass.

question: How does increased mass affect the landing distance?

options.text: It decreases it, because braking improves
Longer, but less than take-off distance
It increases it more than mass increases the take-off distance

explanation: More mass raises VREF and reduces deceleration, but also increases brake drag; the net effect is a longer distance, less marked than for take-off.

question: Why can increased mass partly help braking?

options.text: More wheel load, more brake drag
It reduces the touchdown speed for the same flap setting

explanation: More load on the wheels increases the friction available for braking, if the brakes are not torque-limited, partly offsetting the higher speed and inertia.

question: How does low air density affect the landing distance?

options.text: It decreases it, because drag is lower
It increases it, mainly through more residual thrust

explanation: In thin air, the same IAS means a higher TAS, so there is more speed to lose. The effect is smaller than for the take-off.

question: What wind components must be assumed when calculating landing distance?

options.text: 150% of the headwind and only 50% of the tailwind

explanation: As for take-off, at most 50% of the headwind and at least 150% of the tailwind are used. Most landing charts include this.

question: Is any safety factor applied for crosswind in the landing distance calculation?

options.text: Yes; 150% of the crosswind is used
Yes; 50% of the crosswind is added as a tailwind
No; aeroplanes have crosswind limits instead
Yes; 10% is added to the distance

explanation: There is no factor for crosswind in landing distance; instead the aeroplane has demonstrated crosswind limits.

question: Which flap setting gives the shortest landing distance?
explanation: Full flap gives the lowest approach speed and the most aerodynamic drag, so the landing distance is least and the landing mass can be greatest.

question: What is the disadvantage of landing with full flap?
explanation: Large flap angles greatly reduce climb performance, so in a go-around flaps should be retracted as prescribed once the climb is established.

question: How does an upslope affect the landing distance?

options.text: It reduces it only on wet runways

explanation: On an upslope a component of weight acts backwards, adding to the deceleration and shortening the landing distance.

question: As a rule of thumb, how much does each 1% of downslope change the landing distance?
explanation: Roughly, every 1% of slope changes the landing distance by 5% (a factor of 1.05), longer on a downslope.

question: A landing distance is 1 500 m on a level runway. Using the rule of thumb, what is it with a 2% downslope?
explanation: 2% downslope → +10%: 1 500 × 1.10 = 1 650 m. Applying 5% only once gives 1 575 m.

question: What is a unidirectional runway?

options.text: A runway with approach lighting at one end only
A runway with a single taxiway
One usable in one direction only

explanation: Some runways can only be used in one direction, often because of slope. Pilots must check that the wind allows a safe landing, since a tailwind may be unavoidable.

question: How does a grass surface affect a light aeroplane's landing distance?

options.text: It reduces it, because of impingement drag

explanation: Grass adds impingement drag but greatly reduces braking friction, so overall the landing distance increases, by about 15% for light aeroplanes.

question: How do contaminants such as slush or standing water affect the landing distance?

options.text: They increase it significantly, mainly by reducing braking friction
They increase it only above the dynamic hydroplaning speed
They have no effect if anti-skid is used
They reduce it, because of impingement drag

explanation: Contaminants add some impingement drag, but their main effect is to reduce friction so the brakes cannot work efficiently, greatly increasing the distance.

question: What is a typical braking coefficient of friction on a dry runway?
explanation: On a dry runway the braking friction coefficient is typically 0.8 to 1.0; on wet, slippery or icy runways it can fall below 0.2.

question: On a flooded or icy runway, roughly how much of the deceleration may come from reverse thrust?
explanation: With very little braking available, aerodynamic drag and reverse thrust become far more important; on flooded or icy runways reverse may provide about 80% of the deceleration.

question: By up to how much can a wet runway increase the average dry landing distance?
explanation: A wet runway can increase the average dry landing distance by as much as 50%.

question: How can the pilot obtain information on runway contamination and braking?

options.text: Only by landing and assessing it personally
From runway condition reports, pilot reports or ATC

explanation: Runway condition information comes from reports such as SNOWTAM, runway state reports, pilot reports or ATC, including braking action.

question: What is dynamic hydroplaning?

options.text: The tyre is lifted off the surface by water pressure at high speed
The tyre skids on steam from a locked wheel
The tyre loses pressure in standing water
The tyre rolls on a thin film of water at a low speed

explanation: In dynamic hydroplaning, water cannot escape from under the tyre, and the tyre is held off the pavement by hydrodynamic force, with almost no braking or steering.

question: What is the formula for the dynamic hydroplaning speed of a rotating tyre?

options.text: 9 × tyre pressure in psi, in knots
√(9 × tyre pressure in psi), in knots

explanation: VP (kt) ≈ 9 √P for a rotating tyre. For a non-rotating tyre the factor is 7.7.

question: A tyre has a pressure of 196 psi. What is its dynamic hydroplaning speed when rotating?
explanation: √196 = 14; 9 × 14 = 126 kt. The non-rotating value is 7.7 × 14 ≈ 108 kt.

question: A tyre has a pressure of 144 psi. Once hydroplaning has started on a non-rotating tyre, below about what speed will it stop?
explanation: For a non-rotating tyre VP ≈ 7.7 √P = 7.7 × 12 ≈ 92 kt. The rotating value is 9 × 12 = 108 kt.

question: Which measure helps prevent dynamic hydroplaning?

options.text: Smoothing the runway surface to drain it

explanation: Grooved tyres, transverse runway grooving, a convex (cambered) runway and a good macro-texture all let water escape from under the tyre.

question: What is viscous hydroplaning?

options.text: A tyre losing grip on dry rubber deposits
A locked tyre skidding on steam
Riding a thin film on a smooth surface
A tyre lifted by deep standing water at high speed on touchdown

explanation: Viscous hydroplaning occurs on a very thin water film on a smooth surface and can happen at much lower speeds than dynamic hydroplaning.

question: How is viscous hydroplaning best prevented?

options.text: By grooving the tyres deeply and raising their pressure

explanation: A micro-texture breaks up the thin film so the tyre sits on the peaks of the surface rather than on the water.

question: What causes reverted rubber hydroplaning?

options.text: Deep standing water at high speed
A thin water film on a smooth runway
Rubber deposits left on the runway by previous landings
A prolonged locked-wheel skid that makes steam under the tyre

explanation: A long locked-wheel skid heats the tyre, turning the water underneath into steam that lifts the tyre. The rubber reverts to a sticky deposit.

question: Why is reverted rubber hydroplaning rare in modern airliners?

options.text: Pilots no longer use the brakes
Modern tyres cannot overheat however long they skid

explanation: Reverted rubber hydroplaning needs a locked wheel. Anti-skid braking prevents wheel lock-up and so prevents it.

question: Which landing technique is recommended on a slippery runway?

options.text: Landing 10 kt above VREF to keep control
A firm touchdown at VREF within the touchdown zone
Holding the nose wheel off the runway as long as possible
A long, gentle flare for a smooth touchdown

explanation: A firm touchdown in the touchdown zone loads the wheels, squeezes water out from the footprint and starts auto-spoilers and auto-brakes promptly.

question: Without anti-skid, when should wheel brakes be applied on a wet runway?

options.text: Only after reverse thrust is cancelled

explanation: Without anti-skid the brakes should only be applied below the dynamic hydroplaning speed; with anti-skid they may be applied above it.

question: After main-wheel touchdown on a slippery runway, what should the pilot do with the nose wheel?

options.text: Hold it off as long as possible
Lower it only after reverse thrust
Keep full back pressure until 60 kt
Fly it smoothly onto the runway

explanation: Holding the nose up delays braking and steering. Relaxing back pressure to fly the nose wheel down helps the brakes work early.

question: During a microburst encounter on approach, what is usually experienced first?

options.text: An airspeed increase and a rise above the glide path
An airspeed decrease and a sink below the glide path

explanation: The aeroplane first meets the outflow as a headwind, gaining airspeed and rising above the path, before the downdraught and tailwind.

question: What should a pilot do at the first warning of a microburst on approach?

options.text: Go around at once with full power
Reduce power to regain the glide path
Extend more flap to slow down
Continue and land faster than VREF

explanation: The initial gain in airspeed is the warning. A go-around with full power and a high pitch attitude (around 15°, up to stick shaker) should begin at once.

question: Which visible sign may warn of a microburst?
explanation: Virga, or fallstreaks, is precipitation falling but evaporating before reaching the ground, a sign of strong cooling and downdraughts.

question: Which phase of flight is most vulnerable to severe weather such as windshear?
explanation: Low height, low speed, low thrust and high drag make the landing the most vulnerable phase.
